newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CELTIC AND RANGERS RIVALRY UNEQUALLED.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-CELTIC AND RANGERS RIVALRY UNEQUALLED.

text.p: When Rangers play Celtic two worlds collide.
It has been that way since their first-ever clash in 1888 and it will be that way if football is still played in a thousand years time.
In some families, team loyalties are often split with one brother supporting Liverpool and another Everton, or a father supporting AC Milan while everyone else is cheering for Inter.

That does not happen where Rangers and Celtic are concerned. For their rivalry does not split families, it unites communities. In general terms it has bound Catholics to Celtic and Protestants to Rangers.
In Scottish terms, it is the interloper against the establishment but to those who follow the clubs with all- consuming blind bigotry and passion, it is about far more than a football match.
For the past century or more Rangers have been seen as an embodiment of the Scottish establishment in terms of religion, social status and aspirations.

Celtic, which started life as a charity providing clothes, soup and succour to the poor Catholic families of Glasgow's impoverished East End, were viewed as unwelcome immigrants from Ireland, perceived to be looking to impose their beliefs in a country sure of its rules and regulations.

But while Celtic embraced the community and even enjoyed the greatest-ever period in their history under Protestant manager Jock Stein, Rangers stood firm in their beliefs and no high- profile Catholic player ever pulled on a blue Rangers jersey until then-manager Graeme Souness signed Maurice Johnston in 1989 -- almost 120 years after the club was formed.
"Rangers are a football club and an organisation who are at the very heart of the Scottish establishment," say Bob Ferrier and Robert McElroy in a lavish new history of the club.

"Their place in the very culture of the nation being as distinctive as that of the Church of Scotland, the Scottish legal system, the Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews. Their position in society (emerges) from the historic process that embraced the Masonic Order, the end of the Stuart dynasty of kings, all the way back, if you please, to the Reformation."
Celtic are nothing like that. They were formed by a priest, Brother Walfrid, in 1888 as a means of raising charity money to help the poor Catholic brethern living in Glasgow's slums.

The Irish had been gravitating to Glasgow since the Potato Famine of the 1840s and were unwelcome. The mainly Protestant work force felt their jobs were in peril to these interlopers who would work for less money, so needy were they.

By the turn of the century, both clubs' biggest attendances were reserved for the visit of their arch-rivals, which is how their rivalry became known as the Old Firm. It was an ironic writer who penned the phrase saying the intense rivalry was good business for the old firm.
On the field, as well as off, the passion and loathing have few comparisons in world soccer and one player and many fans have died in the name of the Old Firm.

The player was Celtic's 23-year-old goalkeeper John Thomson who never regained consciousness after an accidental collision when he dived at the feet of Rangers forward Sam English at Ibrox on September 5 1931.

For a few months after his death, rival supporters showed an unusual amount of respect to those of the other club but that did not last long. By the time of their next clash, their rivalry was as bitter as ever -- and has remained so.
The other great tragedy in Old Firm history occurred on January 2, 1971, when 66 fans were crushed to death and 145 injured.
Fans leaving Ibrox tripped and fell over each other after a last-minute Rangers equaliser. That tragedy was instrumental in the later rebuilding of Ibrox in to one of Britain's great stadiums.

In 1909 severe rioting followed two drawn Scottish F.A. Cup final matches and the trophy was withheld from both teams. After the 1980 Scottish Cup final the fans of both clubs fought a pitched battle at Hampden Park after Celtic won the Cup with a late goal.
In a 1987 match tempers flared on the pitch so badly that four players ended up before the Sherriff's Court in Glasgow to answer charges.
Between them the two clubs have dominated Scottish football to an extent not seen in any other country except perhaps in Portugal during the years when Benfica and Sporting Lisbon were all-powerful.

And, as is usual, there is a greater prize at stake than just winning a football match when the two clash at Celtic on Sunday. Rangers are on the verge of equalling Celtic's record run of nine successive league titles, achieved between 1965 and 1974.
A win for Rangers would almost certainly give them their ninth success. Celtic showed last week that they can beat Rangers when they won their Scottish Cup quarter-final 2-0 at home.

But they showed their inconsistency by losing 2-0 to Kilmarnock on Tuesday. As always, the outcome is in some doubt. The only thing you can take for granted is that the passion, emotion and atmosphere will be like no other.
